key_finding: A nudge that shrouded the minimum-payment autopay option cut minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, because nudged users picked autopay amounts barely above the minimum and some lost autopay protection, increasing missed payments.
methodology: Field experiment on live credit card accounts with 6-month follow-up on payment behavior and debt outcomes.
why_it_matters: Directly supports the support team's concern: a choice-architecture change can move a headline enrollment/behavior metric without moving the thing that actually matters (debt/savings amount), and can create new harm (missed payments) for liquidity-constrained users — exactly the trade-off the round-up entry decision must weigh.
limitations: credit card debt paydown, not a savings product
does not test opt-out vs opt-in vs active-choice framing directly, only a shrouding nudge
relevance_reason: A rare consumer-financial field experiment showing a default-like nudge changes nominal behavior without changing the real outcome, with heterogeneity by liquidity — the closest analogue to the brief's core worry.

key_finding: Synthesizes plan-design literature: automatic enrollment and default investment options raise short-term participation but can suppress long-term engagement, and framing of plan features materially shapes behavior.
methodology: Narrative state-of-the-art review of defined-contribution plan design; abstract-only detail on findings.
why_it_matters: Gives a current (2024) map of what the DC-plan literature now believes about engagement costs of defaults, useful as background context but not itself decision-grade for a consumer app.
limitations: entirely employer-sponsored retirement plan setting
no consumer fintech or liquid-savings evidence
abstract gives no effect sizes
relevance_reason: Recent overview of the analogous employer-plan literature the brief says is relevant only by analogy; useful context, capped by domain mismatch.

key_finding: Argues default enrollment raises short-term participation but induces long-term passivity — low contribution rates, inactive account management, and account churn — so participation alone is insufficient evidence of welfare gain.
methodology: Narrative policy commentary synthesizing prior empirical findings on retirement default enrollment; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: States plainly, in policy terms, the exact objection the support team raises about vanity enrollment — but only for retirement accounts, and with no primary data of its own.
limitations: employer/government retirement plan setting, not consumer app
no original data, zero citations, low-authority venue
relevance_reason: Explicitly frames the 'passive trap' critique of default enrollment that mirrors the brief's counter-argument.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and theoretical framework for downstream (post-adoption) default effects, showing they depend on time course of choice/consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and salience of trade-offs — resolving inconsistent prior findings.
methodology: Conceptual synthesis and framework-building across the consumer default-effects literature; abstract-only for empirical specifics.
why_it_matters: Gives the team a structured way to predict and measure which users will disengage after opt-out enrollment (weak antecedent preference, low salience) versus which will actually use the pot — directly shapes what to instrument and watch for in the round-up rollout.
limitations: general consumer choice-architecture theory, not financial-product specific
no effect sizes since it's a conceptual synthesis, not primary data
relevance_reason: The literature's own general-purpose framework for exactly the persistence/disengagement question the brief asks about, in a consumer (not employer) frame.

key_finding: Default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization, and beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive even when the default option causes substantial welfare losses; active choice appears driven by random transitory attention rather than stable attentiveness.
methodology: Three natural experiments using random assignment to default options in Medicare Part D administrative data.
why_it_matters: Strong evidence that default persistence is not conditional on the default being a good fit — relevant to whether an opt-out round-up default will keep unsuitable users enrolled regardless of harm, and that 'active choosers' may just be randomly attentive rather than genuinely engaged.
limitations: health insurance for low-income beneficiaries, not a consumer financial/savings product
no employer-vs-consumer distinction is discussed
relevance_reason: Rigorous natural-experiment evidence on default persistence and the fragility of active choice, useful by analogy though outside the financial-product domain.

key_finding: Across nine 401(k) plans, automatic enrollment raises steady-state savings rates by only 0.6% of income and default auto-escalation by only 0.3%, once job turnover, pre-vesting withdrawals, and auto-escalation opt-outs are accounted for; only 40% of defaulted employees escalate on the first scheduled date.
methodology: Longitudinal administrative data analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating employee separation, balance withdrawal, and auto-escalation opt-out dynamics.
why_it_matters: Directly undercuts the 'defaults will lift enrolment, full stop' argument by showing medium/long-run leakage erodes most of the headline effect — the single best quantified rebuttal to the internal pro-default argument, even though the mechanism (vesting, job turnover) doesn't map onto a liquid consumer app.
limitations: 401(k) retirement plans with employer vesting and job-turnover dynamics that don't exist in a consumer savings app
does not study opt-in or active-choice designs, only opt-out and auto-escalation
relevance_reason: The clearest quantified statement that default effects shrink substantially over time, matching the brief's explicit request for a paper contradicting the 'defaults always help' premise.

key_finding: Germany's nationwide auto-enrollment for low-income employees raised pension participation by 23 percentage points, but most affected individuals actively opted out, and the default effect was strongest among those with high enrollment incentives and low awareness of their enrollment status.
methodology: Natural experiment using administrative and survey data around a nationwide policy introduction of pension auto-enrollment.
why_it_matters: Shows default effect size is highly moderated by incentive salience and knowledge of enrollment status — relevant to predicting whether an opt-out round-up default will 'stick' or be reversed once users notice it, and to who is helped vs. unaffected.
limitations: public pay-as-you-go pension system, government/employer-mediated, not a consumer fintech app
no data on amounts saved or persistence beyond initial opt-out decision
relevance_reason: Recent, large-scale default-effect estimate with explicit heterogeneity by awareness and incentive strength, directly informing distributional questions.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's boost to participation and contributions, replicated at 12 months across 100+ US plans and a UK panel, is substantially attenuated by 36 months, with only modest average savings gains at the longer horizon though inequality in savings is reduced; a life-cycle model fits the pattern with a switching cost of about $250.
methodology: Administrative panel data from over 100 US retirement plans plus a representative UK panel; structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Directly answers the brief's persistence question with a specific horizon comparison (12 vs. 36 months), showing the default effect on amounts saved (not just nominal enrollment) shrinks over time even as it narrows inequality — a nuanced version of the 'vanity enrollment' concern.
limitations: retirement plan context with a $250 switching-cost estimate specific to that setting
no employer-vs-consumer mechanism discussion
relevance_reason: Gives a quantified medium-run attenuation estimate exactly matching the brief's request for whether default effects persist at 6-12+ months and whether they change amounts saved.

key_finding: Across three experiments including a 4,207-person sample from five European countries, default nudges significantly shift risk-taking with medium-to-large effect sizes, but implementing a default (especially one the target refuses) significantly lowers how trustworthy/honest the advice is rated, an effect mediated by perceived wealth-manager honesty.
methodology: Three experiments, including a large representative multi-country European survey experiment on wealth-management default framing and question wording.
why_it_matters: Gives EU-representative evidence that a default which is refused or one-size-fits-all reads as less honest — the exact dark-pattern/reputational risk the brief flags — and shows question framing (e.g., 'how much to invest' vs 'how much to leave safe') independently shifts choices, directly informing both the entry-design and slider-wording decisions.
limitations: wealth-management risk-allocation decisions, not round-up savings specifically
does not measure long-run behavioral persistence, only immediate choice and perception
relevance_reason: EU consumer financial-advice setting testing exactly when a default feels helpful versus manipulative, with quantified reputational costs — the most directly usable evidence for the entry-design decision.

key_finding: Automatic enrollment pushed 401(k) participation above 85% at three firms, but about 80% of participants initially accepted both the low default savings rate (2-3%) and conservative default fund, and half still did so after three years, with offsetting effects on wealth accumulation.
methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large firms' 401(k) plans.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that a pre-set default level anchors most people at that exact level for years — the direct precedent for worrying that a pre-selected round-up multiplier will anchor most users rather than let them choose their true preferred level.
limitations: employer 401(k) plan with employer-selected defaults, not a consumer app
predates the fintech/EU regulatory context the brief says has since changed
relevance_reason: The classic anchoring-on-default-level study the current literature still argues with; directly informs the level/preset decision even though the setting is dated and employer-based.

key_finding: In 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping decisions, 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of a deviation cost and an opt-out cost together (friction complementarity); adding a 15% tip option to the 20/25/30% menu captures 69% of achievable consumer welfare gain at only 5.4% revenue cost.
methodology: Structural model estimated on 8.6 million transaction records plus an independent stated-preference survey to identify true preferences separate from default influence.
why_it_matters: Provides a transferable method — a structural decomposition of why people accept a preset menu option and a counterfactual tool for choosing which value to add/preset — directly applicable to deciding which round-up multiplier (1x/2x/5x) to preset and what a welfare-minimizing menu looks like.
limitations: tipping decisions, not a financial savings product
no persistence or longitudinal outcome measured, single-decision setting
relevance_reason: Explicit method transfer: a structural friction/menu-design model for preset-option adherence and welfare trade-offs, directly usable for the multiplier-level decision even though the underlying transactions are taxi tips.

key_finding: An opt-in payroll-deduction short-term savings account (withdrawable anytime) at five UK firms saw only 0.7% of eligible employees ever activate it, but among activators, 96% still had a positive balance and 87% received an automatic contribution at 12 months.
methodology: Field study of a choice-architecture intervention introducing opt-in short-term savings accounts at five UK employers, with 12-month account-level tracking.
why_it_matters: The closest existing product analogue to the round-up feature (liquid, withdrawable savings) shows opt-in produces very low take-up but very high persistence among adopters — the strongest available evidence for the trade-off between opt-in's low volume and opt-out's engagement risk, though it runs through an employer payroll channel.
limitations: employer-mediated payroll deduction, not a self-directed consumer app enrollment
does not test opt-out or active-choice designs for comparison
relevance_reason: A liquid short-term savings product almost identical to round-up savings, directly informing the opt-in enrollment volume vs. persistence trade-off, despite the employer distribution channel.

key_finding: Characterizes optimal default options generally: when designer and choosers agree on an activity's value, weighted opt-out minimization is asymptotically optimal, with extensions for Pigouvian fees and cases of designer-chooser disagreement over value.
methodology: Theoretical economic model with asymptotic analysis and numerical simulations; abstract-only for specifics.
why_it_matters: A general normative framework for when minimizing opt-outs (i.e., choosing an opt-out enrollment design) is actually optimal versus when designer and user preferences diverge — useful for reasoning about when an opt-out round-up default is welfare-improving versus manipulative, though it offers no product-specific numbers.
limitations: purely theoretical/simulation-based, no empirical validation in any consumer or financial setting
does not specify a population or setting to compare against the brief's context
relevance_reason: General optimal-default theory bearing on when an opt-out design serves users versus the designer, relevant to the manipulation-risk question even without domain-specific data.

key_finding: Maps EU laws on dark patterns to a taxonomy of six autonomy-violation categories, showing EU regulation of pre-selected defaults and similar practices is grounded in protecting consumer autonomy.
methodology: Legal/doctrinal analysis and normative taxonomy construction; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Directly informs whether an opt-out enrollment design risks being classified as a dark pattern under EU law, which should shape the choice between opt-out and active-choice designs.
limitations: legal/normative analysis, not empirical
no effect sizes on enrollment or engagement
not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: Gives the EU regulatory framework for judging whether a default reads as helpful or manipulative, the reputational risk the brief flags explicitly.

key_finding: With a 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees had not opted out after 12 months (versus ~50% non-opt-out under lower defaults elsewhere), and non-opters anchored at an income-suboptimal 12% rate.
methodology: Administrative panel data from a firm with an unusually high default contribution rate; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Shows the default level itself shapes both enrollment persistence and anchoring, evidence for how a high pre-set round-up multiplier could both raise and distort savings behavior.
limitations: employer-sponsored 401(k) plan, not a consumer app
single-firm case study
relevance_reason: Directly tests anchoring on a high default level and 12-month opt-out persistence, close in structure to the round-up multiplier decision even though the setting is a retirement plan.

key_finding: Abstract text unavailable; title indicates four large UK field experiments on automating short-term payroll savings.
methodology: abstract-only; described as field experiments, details unavailable.
why_it_matters: Could speak to automatic enrollment in short-term, more liquid savings vehicles closer to the round-up product than retirement plans, but content cannot be verified from the truncated abstract.
limitations: abstract truncated/unavailable, so specific findings cannot be assessed
unclear whether savings are liquid or locked
relevance_reason: Title suggests short-term payroll savings automation experiments, potentially closer to the round-up feature's liquidity than retirement studies, but evidence cannot be confirmed.

key_finding: At-scale UK bank field experiments show automatic enrollment into just-in-time overdraft text alerts cuts unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, implying market-wide savings of £170-240 million.
methodology: Large-scale randomized field experiments at major UK banks.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates that automatic (opt-out style) enrollment into a low-friction banking feature produces large, quantifiable consumer financial benefits in the exact UK consumer-banking setting the round-up feature will operate in.
limitations: studies alert enrollment, not a savings contribution decision
does not report the alert feature's own disengagement or opt-out rate
relevance_reason: Same consumer-banking, self-directed, field-experiment setting as the product being built, showing default enrollment into a bank feature at scale changes real financial outcomes.

key_finding: Automatic pension enrollment increased average savings by £32-38/month over 41 months but was partially offset by a £7/month rise in unsecured debt and higher mortgage balances, though loan defaults fell and credit scores rose modestly.
methodology: Randomized policy roll-out across ~160,000 UK employers with 2-29 employees; administrative panel data, 41-month follow-up.
why_it_matters: Directly undercuts the 'defaults always help' premise: some of the extra savings generated by automatic enrollment leak out as extra debt, meaning nominal enrollment gains can overstate net financial benefit.
limitations: employer-mediated pension context, not a consumer app
measures debt offset for retirement savings, not liquid round-up savings
relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the assumption that default-driven savings increases are a pure win, showing offsetting debt effects — relevant to whether opt-out enrollment produces real versus vanity savings gains.

key_finding: Removing an auto-enrollment policy and adding a minor application 'ordeal' step reduced health insurance enrollment by 33%, differentially excluding young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged people.
methodology: Natural experiment studying removal of an auto-enrollment policy in a health insurance selection market.
why_it_matters: Shows that friction removed by opt-out defaults protects exactly the populations least likely to actively opt in, informing the brief's concern about who is helped versus hurt by enrollment design.
limitations: health insurance selection market, not a savings product
adverse selection dynamics specific to insurance may not apply to savings
relevance_reason: Quantifies how much friction (the opposite of a default) excludes disadvantaged users, directly informing the distributional question of who opt-in enrollment would leave out.

key_finding: Using 41 million observations, automatic (passive) employer contributions raise total saving substantially, while active-choice tax subsidies induce only about 1 cent of extra saving per $1 of subsidy, because 85% of individuals are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies.
methodology: Population-level Danish administrative panel data on savings and retirement accounts.
why_it_matters: The foundational large-scale evidence for the passive-versus-active savings distinction underlying the internal 'defaults lift enrolment' argument, though drawn from a tax-subsidy retirement context.
limitations: retirement accounts with government tax subsidies, not a consumer app
outside the 2020s app/regulatory context the brief says has changed the calculus
relevance_reason: Provides the classic large-N evidence for the passive-versus-active savings distinction underlying the active-choice design question, which current work in this space still argues with.

key_finding: Field experiments show 'active choice' (a forced yes/no decision with no default) and a proposed 'enhanced active choice' that highlights losses from the non-preferred option can motivate behavior change as an alternative to automatic enrollment.
methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice designs; abstract gives no quantified effect sizes.
why_it_matters: Directly tests the third onboarding option in the brief (forced active choice) and proposes a refinement that nudges the choice while preserving user agency, relevant to whether active choice can capture most of the enrollment benefit without an outright default.
limitations: medication-adherence and general behavior-change focus rather than consumer financial products
no quantified enrollment or persistence numbers in the abstract
relevance_reason: The originating study of the 'active choice' and 'enhanced active choice' concepts the brief is directly weighing as a third onboarding option.

key_finding: A review of household financial behavior and interventions — education, peer effects, product design, advice/disclosure, and choice architecture — summarizes which levers shift savings, borrowing, and payment behavior.
methodology: Narrative review/book chapter synthesizing empirical household finance literature; abstract-only, no numeric effect sizes given.
why_it_matters: Offers a broad synthesis of which choice-architecture levers (including defaults) move household financial behavior, useful as a map of the evidence base rather than a specific effect size for this decision.
limitations: overview chapter with no default-specific effect sizes in the abstract
covers many financial domains, not specifically round-up or app-based savings
relevance_reason: The review-level synthesis of behavioral household finance interventions the brief asked for, situating the round-up decision within the broader choice-architecture evidence base.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment raised participation above 85% at three firms, but about 80% of participants accepted the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and default fund, with half still at the default after three years.
methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large firms comparing automatic versus standard enrollment.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that defaults both massively raise nominal enrollment and strongly anchor the contribution level for years, directly the tension the brief poses between enrollment lift and just relocating people to a low pre-set level.
limitations: employer-sponsored 401(k), not a consumer app
pre-dates the mobile/EU regulatory context the brief says has changed the calculus
relevance_reason: The foundational default-and-anchoring study that all subsequent enrollment-design literature, including this project's question, argues with or extends.

key_finding: Randomly assigning default enrollment into a salary-linked savings account increased participation by 40 percentage points, equivalent to a 50% matching incentive, driven mainly by present-biased preferences and the cognitive cost of choosing.
methodology: Randomized field experiment with salary-linked savings accounts and a series of mechanism-isolating interventions.
why_it_matters: Identifies the psychological mechanism (cognitive cost, present bias) behind why defaults work, and shows default assignment can increase later active saving — evidence for whether an opt-out default would just be nominal or would build lasting saving habits.
limitations: salary-linked savings account administered through an employer, not an independent consumer app
very different economic/regulatory context (Afghanistan) from the EU
relevance_reason: Provides mechanism-level evidence for why defaults change savings behavior, useful for judging whether opt-out enrollment would produce real engagement or just nominal sign-up.

key_finding: A randomized nudge (credit card payment reminders) on a Brazilian financial management platform cut late-payment fees by 14% but raised overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use experiencing a net 5% fee increase while other users saved 15%.
methodology: Randomized field experiment with a consumer financial management platform in Brazil.
why_it_matters: Shows a well-intentioned nudge in a consumer fintech app can help most users while making a vulnerable subgroup worse off, directly the distributional risk the brief warns against building for on average.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrollment defaults or round-up savings specifically
single-country consumer credit context, not an EU savings app
relevance_reason: A closely analogous fintech field experiment showing heterogeneous, sometimes harmful, effects of a helpful-seeming nudge — exactly the distributional risk the brief asks the team to check for before defaulting everyone in.
